planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil under dappled to moderate shade; the slow-creeping rhizomes fill in a patch over one to two growing seasons.

directions: Native from the Carolinas west to Texas over calcareous soils, this fine-textured, weeping evergreen sedge forms a slow-spreading patch in exactly the dry-to-moist deciduous shade found under live oak canopy. Plant in humus-rich, near-neutral soil with some dappled light for the best fullness, and avoid piling mulch over the crown. Once rooted in, established clumps tolerate the dry summer shade typical under oak canopy without supplemental water. Cut back old foliage in late winter just before new growth emerges to keep the fountain-like form tidy.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery / Juniper Level Botanic Garden
Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Divide established clumps in spring or fall and set into consistently moist, organically rich soil in full shade to dappled light, mimicking bottomland hardwood floor conditions.

directions: Native specifically to rich bottomland forests from the Florida panhandle and southern Mississippi west to Texas, lined sedge is a true Gulf Coast counterpart to the Appalachian and Piedmont Carex species that dominate the trade. Site it in consistently moist, organically rich soil in full shade and top-dress yearly with leaf litter rather than bark mulch to match its native nutrient cycle. It does not tolerate prolonged drought, so it performs best under canopy where leaf litter holds moisture through the summer. Divide congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigor and fullness.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Divide the densely clumped crown in spring and plant into constantly moist to boggy, acidic, sandy soil in full shade; avoid letting the site dry out between waterings.

directions: Native to acidic, sandy forested swamps across the Southeast coastal plain including Florida, Georgia, and Mississippi, this sedge fills the boggy, deep-shade swale under live oak and pine canopy where standing water and shade combine, a spot most garden sedges can't handle. Give it constantly moist to boggy, acidic, sandy soil in full shade, such as a low point in a rain garden or a natural seep. Combine it with cinnamon fern or swamp doghobble for a naturalistic acidic-swamp planting. This is a true wetland-margin species, so it is not a fit for average garden soil that dries between rains.
sources: Florida Plant Atlas (University of South Florida)

planting.note: Divide the rhizomatous clump in spring and plant into consistently moist to wet, organically rich soil at the part-shade edge of a pond, ditch, or rain garden.

directions: One of the few goldenrods that genuinely performs in part shade, this species naturally grows at marsh edges and open woodland seeps, giving Gulf Coast gardeners a native fall pollinator plant for the dappled-light zone where sun-loving goldenrods decline. Give it consistently moist to wet, rich soil at a pond, ditch, or rain-garden margin and room to spread gently via rhizomes, since it colonizes rather than runs aggressively. Deadhead or cut back after bloom to limit self-seeding in smaller beds, and pair it with swamp doghobble and native sedges in a shaded wet-margin planting.

subcategory: upland Gulf South woodland shade perennial

planting.note: Sow fresh seed outdoors in a cold frame in fall for natural stratification ahead of spring germination, or divide short rhizomes in spring or fall; plant into humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in full shade.

directions: A woodland-floor perennial reaching into Alabama and Mississippi, large-leaf waterleaf offers cream late-spring flower clusters and bold, hairy foliage that holds up through summer shade — a genuine addition to Southeast shade-wildflower collections. This mesic cove-forest species wants humus-rich, consistently moist soil in full shade and declines in sites that dry out or catch afternoon sun, so it suits inland Gulf South woodland gardens with cooler soil better than sandy, immediate-coastal sites. It spreads slowly via short rhizomes into a loose colony rather than an aggressive mat, and pairs well with other calcareous-leaning shade perennials.
